lesson.title: Energy of motion

steps.headline: Kinetic energy is ½mv²: the energy a moving object has because of its speed.

lead.text: Kinetic energy depends on the mass and on the square of the speed. It is never negative, and it does not depend on direction.
A 2 kg cart moves at 3 m/s.

reveal.text: You squared the speed, multiplied by the mass and halved it: ½ × 2 × 9 gives 9 J.

steps.headline: A 1 kg ball speeds up from 2 m/s to 4 m/s. Compare its kinetic energies.

workedSteps.text: Divide the new energy by the old.

steps.headline: A cart's speed doubles and its mass stays the same. By what factor does the kinetic energy change?

workedSteps.text: Mass is fixed, so only v² can change.
Replace v with 2v and square it.

steps.headline: The net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy.

lead.text: A net force that speeds an object up does positive net work. One that slows it down does negative net work.
A 2 kg cart is pushed until it goes faster. Find the energy at each speed first.

reveal.text: Net work is the gain in kinetic energy, from 9 J to 25 J.

lead.text: Keep the speed fixed and change the mass instead.

reveal.text: Mass enters ½mv² once, so energy scales with mass directly. Speed is the term that is squared.

lesson.orientation: Use kinetic energy and net work to connect force with a change in speed.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Brakes stop a bike from 3 m/s in 1 m.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find kinetic energy and see how net work changes it.

recap.keyIdea: Kinetic energy is ½mv², so it grows with the square of the speed. Net work equals the change in kinetic energy.

blocks.text: You found that a bike at twice the speed needs four times the stopping distance, and that speeding a 2 kg cart from 3 m/s to 5 m/s takes 16 J of net work.

recap.nextHook: Height stores energy too. How much?

questions.prompt: A 2 kg cart moves at 3 m/s. Find its kinetic energy in joules.
hints: Kinetic energy uses speed squared.
Use K = ½mv².
Square the speed, multiply by mass, then take half.
questions.onCorrect: 9 J. Square the speed first, then multiply by the mass and take half.

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves out the half. Kinetic energy is ½mv².
That squares the product of mass and speed instead of the speed alone.
That is the speed. Kinetic energy is ½mv².

questions.prompt: A cart's speed doubles while its mass stays fixed. By what factor does its kinetic energy increase?
hints: Mass is fixed, so only the speed term changes.
Doubling the speed doubles v before it is squared.
Square the 2.
questions.onCorrect: 4. The speed is squared, so doubling it multiplies kinetic energy by four.

misconceptions.feedback: That scales energy with speed. Kinetic energy depends on speed squared.
That would be speed cubed. Energy goes as speed squared.

questions.prompt: A cart's mass doubles while its speed stays fixed. What happens to its kinetic energy?
hints: Separate the first power of mass from the square of speed.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Mass enters K = ½mv² as a direct multiplier, so energy doubles.

questions.onCorrect: It doubles. Mass multiplies directly in ½mv², so twice the mass is twice the energy.

misconceptions.feedback: More mass at the same speed means more energy, not less.
Squaring applies to the speed, not the mass. Doubling the mass doubles the energy.

questions.prompt: A 2 kg cart speeds up from 3 m/s to 5 m/s. Find the net work done on it in joules.
hints: Calculate the final and initial kinetic energies.
Net work equals their difference.
Calculate 25 − 9.
questions.onCorrect: 16 J. Net work equals the change in kinetic energy: final minus initial.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the final kinetic energy alone. Net work is the change: final minus initial.
That uses the change in speed. Work is the change in ½mv².

questions.prompt: A 4 kg object moves at speed 5 m/s. Find its kinetic energy in joules.
hints: Square speed before multiplying.
Use the one-half factor.
Calculate 0.5 × 4 × 25.
questions.onCorrect: 50 J. Square the speed, multiply by the mass, take half.

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves out the half. Kinetic energy is ½mv².
That uses the speed without squaring it.

questions.prompt: A cart initially has 50 J of kinetic energy and comes to rest. What net work is done on it?
hints: Use the energy change, including its sign.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Net work is final minus initial kinetic energy: 0 − 50 = −50 J.

questions.onCorrect: A loss of fifty joules. Net work is final minus initial kinetic energy: 0 − 50.

misconceptions.feedback: The cart lost energy, so the net work is negative, not a gain.
Its kinetic energy changed, so the net work is not zero. Net work equals that change.

questions.prompt: The same brakes stop it from 6 m/s in how many metres?
hints: Does twice the speed mean twice the distance?
Think about how the energy to be removed grows with speed.
Squaring the speed makes the energy, and the distance, grow faster than the speed.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Twice the speed means four times the energy to remove, so 4 m.

questions.onCorrect: 4 m. Twice the speed needs four times the stopping distance. The reason is kinetic energy, which depends on speed squared.

misconceptions.feedback: That doubles the distance with the speed. The energy to remove grows faster than that.

questions.prompt: A 1 kg ball moves at 6 m/s. What is its kinetic energy in joules?
hints: Square the speed first.
Multiply by the mass.
Take half of the result.

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves out the half.
That is the speed. Square it, multiply by the mass and halve.

questions.prompt: Why does kinetic energy go up by more than the speed does?
hints: Read each choice against the situation before you answer.

acceptedIdeas: The speed is squared in ½mv².
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The speed is squared in ½mv².

choices.label: The speed is squared in ½mv².

questions.onCorrect: Speed is squared, so doubling it quadruples the energy.

misconceptions.feedback: The mass is fixed here. Only the speed changes.
Speed is the heart of the formula: K = ½mv².

questions.prompt: A cart's kinetic energy rises from 10 J to 25 J. What net work was done on it, in joules?
hints: Net work is the change in kinetic energy.
Final minus initial.
Take the first value from the second.
questions.onCorrect: 15 J. Net work equals the change in kinetic energy.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two energies. Net work is the change: final minus initial.
The energy rose, so the net work is positive.

questions.prompt: A 2 kg cart slows from 5 m/s to 1 m/s. What net work is done on it, in joules?
hints: Find the kinetic energy before and after.
Net work is final minus initial.
The cart loses energy, so the answer is negative.
questions.onCorrect: −24 J. The cart loses kinetic energy, so the net work is negative.

misconceptions.feedback: The size is right, but the cart slowed. The net work is negative.
That uses the change in speed. Work is the change in ½mv².
